data.title: Kalshi pitches a futures market tied to inflation - report
data.description:
Prediction markets company Kalshi (KALSHI) is pushing further into the territory of traditional financial exchanges by promoting a futures market tied to inflation, according to a media report on Friday.

The company, whose prediction markets platform has surged in popularity, targets launching exchange-traded futures contracts tracking the consumer price index and the closely watched core inflation measure in December, Bloomberg News reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

Kalshi (KALSHI) has been marketing the idea to the world's largest banks and hedge funds, the report said.

The new contracts would be the only futures linked directly to the CPI, offering Kalshi a unique product to attract macro investors active in the multitrillion-dollar markets for interest-rate and bond futures currently offered by CME Group (CME) and Intercontinental Exchange (ICE), the article said.

The company has called on Michael Ashton, a former Barclays (BCS) trader known as the "Inflation Guy," to design the contracts and pique big investment firms' interest.

"There’s no exchange that trades this, and they want to be the inflation exchange," Ashton, the managing principal of Enduring Investments LLC, told Bloomberg.

data.title: CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, Optum Rx targeted in House investigation
data.description:
• The House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform has launched an investigation into whether CVS Caremark (CVS), Express Scripts, and Optum Rx engaged in punitive audits against independent pharmacies as punishment for supporting legislation to reform the pharmacy benefit manager industry.
  • "In the short span of time since the Committee’s July markup of H.R. 6610, the Pharmacists Fight Back in FEHB Plans Act, multiple independent pharmacies that supported the Committee’s efforts have received an unusual number of audit notices for minuscule prescription charges after the stated compliance deadline date from CVS Caremark," Chairman James Comer (R-Ky.) writes in his letter to CVS Caremark.
  • One audit conducted by a PBM was over a drug that cost $0.99 "that resulted in hundreds of hours of staff time for the independent pharmacy," according to a news release.
  • Comer is asking for information from the three PBMs related to audits conducted from July 22 to the present.
  • Express Scripts is owned by Cigna (CI), while Optum Rx is a part of UnitedHealth (UNH).

data.title: Selective outlines 96.5%-97.5% 2026 combined ratio outlook as it raises after-tax net investment income view to $490M
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Selective Insurance Group (SIGI) Q3 2026

Management View

  • CEO John J. Marchioni said results reflected “a 16.9% operating ROE, improved underwriting margins and excellent net investment income, which increased 16% year-over-year,” adding it was the “ninth consecutive quarter of double-digit operating returns.”
  • Marchioni emphasized near-term premium growth trade-offs from portfolio actions: “They have reduced near-term premium growth, but we are prioritizing improved underwriting returns over volume,” and described a sharper renewal mix shift in Standard Commercial Lines as headline rate increases soften.
  • On cohort actions, Marchioni highlighted retention dispersion, stating “retention in our best-performing cohorts remains strong at 90%,” while “retention in our lowest performing cohorts… declined to 52%, down from 79% a year ago,” alongside “renewal pure price increased 17.2%” in that lowest-performing bucket.
  • Marchioni framed E&S as a growth lever, saying the retail access initiative “has moved from build-out to execution,” and added the company is “thoughtfully expand[ing] our brokerage appetite to deepen our long-standing wholesale relationships.”
  • CFO Patrick Brennan reported “fully diluted EPS of $2.11 and non-GAAP operating EPS of $2.37,” and said results “result[ed] in a 15.1% ROE and a 16.9% operating ROE,” with a “GAAP combined ratio… 96.8%, including 5.4 points of catastrophe losses.”
  • Brennan announced increased shareholder returns and authorizations: “we are pleased to announce a 12% increase in our quarterly dividend,” and “our Board authorized a new $200 million share repurchase program,” with “total available repurchase capacity… approximately $253 million.”

Outlook

  • Brennan updated full-year targets: “We continue to expect a GAAP combined ratio between 96.5% and 97.5%, assuming 5.5 points of catastrophe losses, which is down from 6 points a quarter ago,” while adding, “Our assumption for the underlying loss ratio is unchanged from last quarter.”
  • Brennan raised investment income expectations: “We have also increased our expected after-tax net investment income to $490 million, up from $480 million,” and said guidance assumes “an effective tax rate of 21.5%” and “a fully diluted weighted average share count of 59.9 million.”
  • On Hurricane Isaias, Brennan said, “it is too early to provide specific estimates,” but added, “we expect our losses from the event will be immaterial to our results.”

Financial Results

  • Brennan said there was “no prior year casualty reserve development at the segment or line of business level this quarter,” and added, “Reserves in our underlying general liability line have now been stable for 7 consecutive quarters.”
  • On expense levels, Brennan said, “Our 32.1% expense ratio was elevated in the quarter, reflecting in part lower premium volume,” while reiterating, “We continue to expect our full year underwriting expense ratio to be approximately 31.5%.”
  • Brennan said after-tax net investment income was “$127 million in the quarter,” and noted book value impact from markets: “after-tax net unrealized losses… was the primary driver of the 5% decline in book value per common share to $55.02,” while “adjusted book value per common share… increased 2% to $62.”

Q&A

  • Michael Phillips, Oppenheimer: Asked how much commercial accident-year loss ratio improvement came from remediation vs. “normal quarterly variation,” and what “inning” the remediation is in; CEO Marchioni: clarified the “5 points” impact related to “lower retention in our underperforming cohorts… across all commercial lines,” and said the company is “effectively 3 quarters through a full renewal cycle,” while CFO Brennan noted Q3 2025 was a “high” comparison and suggested comparing “full year ’25 to the year-to-date ’26.”
  • Michael Phillips, Oppenheimer: Asked about expense ratio pressures and investment flexibility; CFO Brennan: said Selective intends “to continue to invest,” but must “maintain cost discipline,” and pointed to a premium audit enhancement that “led to some additional premium collection… [but] we did have higher premium write-offs during the quarter.”
  • Rowland Mayor, RBC Capital Markets: Asked for profitability differences between best and worst cohorts; CEO Marchioni: “We’re not going to go into that level of specificity,” but said differences are “meaningful.”
  • Rowland Mayor, RBC Capital Markets: Asked what made buybacks “opportunistic;” CFO Brennan: cited balancing “go-forward view of growth” with buying at “a stock price that we think is attractive,” while CEO Marchioni added management feels “really good about how we’re positioned to restore the growth profile.”
  • Michael Zaremski, BMO: Pressed on whether “opportunistic” implies a valuation range and whether lower growth changes capital needs; CFO Brennan: “I’m not going to forecast where and what we’re going to do,” reiterating buybacks depend on valuation and growth needs; CEO Marchioni said pressured conversion reflects casualty pricing discipline but added, “there are high-quality opportunities out there to be had.”
  • Jon Paul Newsome, Piper Sandler: Asked how E&S strategy navigates a competitive market; CEO Marchioni: said the approach is to increase submissions so “lower conversion rates can be offset by higher submissions,” citing retail expansion and potential appetite expansion such as making “Inland Marine… available to our wholesale partners on a non-admitted basis.”
  • Meyer Shields, KBW: Asked if underwriting action headwinds accelerated and about commercial auto exposure/geography; CEO Marchioni: said “there’s a small acceleration” tied to retention in “low and very low buckets,” and added commercial auto premiums were “down about 11%” in the quarter and “year-to-date, down about 7%,” reflecting lower auto counts and mix shifts.
  • Meyer Shields, KBW: Asked why corporate expenses were low; CFO Brennan: said it was “driven by changes in our long-term incentive plan compensation expense… driven by… our stock price.”

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analysts’ tone was slightly negative to skeptical, focusing on remediation durability, expense leverage, cohort profitability transparency, capital deployment constraints, and near-term growth pressure; examples included requests to quantify cohort profitability (Rowland Mayor, RBC Capital Markets) and repeated probing of “opportunistic” repurchase limits (Michael Zaremski, BMO).
  • Management tone was slightly positive in prepared remarks and more defensive/clarifying in Q&A; CEO Marchioni used corrective framing such as “I just want to make sure I clarify,” and stressed cycle discipline, while maintaining confidence in actions as “the right actions to create long-term value.”
  • Versus last quarter, management leaned more on evidence of execution (cohort retention splits, retail E&S execution) and less on milestone messaging (e.g., headquarters/anniversary in Q2), while analysts remained consistent in pressing on casualty lines, growth trade-offs, and capital returns.

Quarter-over-quarter comparison

  • Guidance language shifted from Q2’s expectation to be “near the top of the range” to Q3’s expectation implied to be “closer to the middle of the range” (CFO Brennan) as the catastrophe loss assumption moved to “5.5 points… down from 6 points a quarter ago.”
  • Standard Commercial mix actions intensified modestly: Q2 described worst-cohort retention falling to “55%,” while Q3 described lowest-performing cohort retention at “52%,” with Marchioni characterizing “a small acceleration” in the low buckets.
  • Capital return posture escalated: Q2 referenced “$32 million of share repurchases” and remaining authorization, while Q3 added “$55 million of opportunistic share repurchases,” a “12% increase” in the quarterly dividend, and a new “$200 million” repurchase authorization.

Risks and Concerns

  • Marchioni said industry conditions heighten risk in casualty: “commercial casualty margins across the industry [are] under pressure and market pricing generally below elevated severity trends,” and warned that disciplined pricing can suppress conversion rates and near-term growth.
  • Brennan flagged expense ratio sensitivity to premium volume, saying the quarterly expense ratio was “elevated… reflecting in part lower premium volume,” while maintaining the full-year expectation.
  • Brennan said Hurricane Isaias estimates were premature: “it is too early to provide specific estimates,” though he added early indicators point to immaterial losses.

Final Takeaway

Management characterized Q3 as a quarter of stronger profitability and capital return actions, pairing a lower catastrophe assumption within the unchanged 96.5%-97.5% combined ratio range with a higher $490 million after-tax net investment income outlook. Leadership emphasized that sharper underwriting and renewal mix actions—particularly in the lowest-performing commercial cohorts—are intentionally pressuring near-term growth while aiming to improve risk-adjusted returns, alongside execution of E&S retail access expansion and continued opportunistic buybacks under expanded authorization.

data.title: Orchid Island outlines high-teens ROE potential as it continues buybacks with shares at >20% discount to book
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Orchid Island Capital (ORC) Q3 2026

Management View

  • "Net income, we posted a net loss of $0.90 per share in Q3 compared to net income of $0.44 in Q2." (VP & Treasurer Jerry Sintes)

  • "Book value at September 30 decreased to $6.02 per share compared to $7.22 at the end of Q2." (VP & Treasurer Sintes)

  • "Total return for the quarter, inclusive of dividends declared, was negative 12.5% for Q3 compared to a positive 6.2% during Q2." (VP & Treasurer Sintes)

  • "And we declared a dividend of $0.30 per share during the quarter, which was consistent with Q2." (VP & Treasurer Sintes)

  • "Obviously, the big story in Q3 was this material sell-off in the rates market that occurred right at the end of the quarter" and management pointed to drivers including "inflation" and "sovereign debt issuance." (Chairman, President & CEO Robert Cauley)

  • "We opted to not do a lot of widespread selling. Instead, we had modest selling and let the prepayments run off and instead address the sell-off by adjusting our hedges." (Chairman, President & CEO Cauley)

  • "We wanted to do our hedging in the futures market more so than swaps just because swap spreads have widened so much" and "we also took the hedge coverage from a pretty high 91% going into the quarter to 99%." (Chairman, President & CEO Cauley)

  • "We repurchased 6.62 million shares since the end of the second quarter, taking advantage of the substantial discount to book in the stock while maintaining a competitive expense ratio and avoiding dilutive equity issuance." (CFO, Chief Investment Officer, Secretary & Management Director George Haas)

Outlook

  • "Looking ahead to the fourth quarter and next year, we'll continue this disciplined approach: We expect to reduce hedges as rates rally, add mortgage assets as market conditions and leverage normalize and look for opportunities to improve portfolio carry as relative value opportunities emerge." (CFO, Chief Investment Officer, Secretary & Management Director Haas)

  • "Our taxable income estimates remain in line with the dividends paid year-to-date" and "a modest increase in asset yields has contributed to some improvement in our taxable net interest margin." (CFO, Chief Investment Officer, Secretary & Management Director Haas)

  • "At current leverage levels, we believe the portfolio is capable of generating returns on equity in the high teens" and management added that "somewhat higher prospective returns" could come from "new investments or selective portfolio rotation." (CFO, Chief Investment Officer, Secretary & Management Director Haas)

  • Compared with Q2’s emphasis on uncertainty around policy and war-related volatility, Q3 commentary highlighted stabilization after quarter-end, including that "we've definitely seen a change in the rates market from what we saw at the end of Q3." (Chairman, President & CEO Cauley)

Financial Results

  • "Our leverage ratio at September 30 was 8.6x compared to 7.3x at June 30" and "our liquidity during -- at the end of Q3 was 44% compared to 54% at the end of Q2." (VP & Treasurer Sintes)

  • "3-month CPR during the quarter was 8.4% compared to 10.9% during Q2." (VP & Treasurer Sintes)

  • "During Q3, we had an average portfolio size of $11.1 billion compared to $11.4 billion in Q2." (VP & Treasurer Sintes)

  • "This improvement has been reflected in our performance, with book value increasing approximately 4.5% month-to-date through yesterday, October 22." (CFO, Chief Investment Officer, Secretary & Management Director Haas)

Q&A

  • Douglas Harter, BTIG: asked whether the 4.5% book value update included dividends/accruals; Chairman, President & CEO Cauley replied, "Yes, yes" to it being an economic return framing, later adding it "reflects the accrual of the earnings, the dividend," while CFO, Chief Investment Officer, Secretary & Management Director Haas clarified, "the dividend has been removed from shareholders' equity."

  • Douglas Harter, BTIG: asked how ORC weighs buybacks vs. buying assets; Chairman, President & CEO Cauley said, "we're comfortably below 80% of book," noted Q4 repurchases were "about 1.7 million," and added, "We will cease. We will start reinvesting paydowns. And we may actually add some assets"; CFO, Chief Investment Officer, Secretary & Management Director Haas said there were portfolio areas that "look more attractive than others" and the company could rotate out of "the tighter things" into coupons "that are more attractive."

  • Jason Weaver, JonesTrading: asked about dividend coverage and comfort with $0.30; Chairman, President & CEO Cauley answered, "we're quite content" and "we are very comfortable with the current pay rate" if conditions and composition hold.

  • Jason Weaver, JonesTrading: asked about a 15/30 coupon swap and whether it was a spread hedge; CFO, Chief Investment Officer, Secretary & Management Director Haas described it as a relative value trade, said it was unwound after it "gapped tighter about 10 ticks," and also explained selling pools and covering a TBA short "has helped us bolster our cash and get the leverage down a little bit."

  • Mikhail Goberman, Citizens JMP: asked about leverage trajectory; Chairman, President & CEO Cauley said leverage "was quite high at the end of the quarter," is "still north of 8x," and added, "our intention now is to retain the portfolio at this size" while "reinvest paydowns" and potentially "add some"; CFO, Chief Investment Officer, Secretary & Management Director Haas updated, "Leverage is at 8.12x," and emphasized being "very well hedged from an interest rate standpoint" while acknowledging "exposure to volatility and mortgage basis."

  • Mikhail Goberman, Citizens JMP: asked whether ORC targets an 8x–8.5x leverage band while buying back stock; Chairman, President & CEO Cauley replied, "Yes, that makes sense," adding buybacks remain compelling if the stock stays "meaningfully below 80% of book," while CFO, Chief Investment Officer, Secretary & Management Director Haas said the firm can sell positions that "don't have to stay" if "the better use of capital is to buy stock back."

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analysts’ tone was neutral and detail-oriented, focusing on mechanics and sustainability—book value accounting, dividend coverage, leverage range, and hedge intent (e.g., "trying to ballpark dividend coverage going forward").

  • Management’s tone was slightly positive on opportunity but guarded on market conditions, with confidence statements on capital actions and payout ("we are very comfortable with the current pay rate") alongside repeated caveats about market uncertainty ("Don't know what will happen in the next few days").

  • Versus Q2, where management emphasized uncertainty around rates and macro developments, Q3 included more explicit post-quarter stabilization signals ("we stabilized"), alongside sharper frustration on valuation constraints ("it's really an albatross around our neck"). (Chairman, President & CEO Cauley)

Quarter-over-quarter Comparison

  • Q3 flipped from Q2’s positive performance to a reported loss and book value decline, with management tying the change to the late-quarter rates sell-off and mortgage basis widening.

  • Hedging posture tightened quarter-over-quarter: Q3 commentary described raising hedge coverage to "99%" and shifting mix toward futures due to wider swap spreads, while Q2 emphasized building swap coverage and discussing funding-cost dynamics.

  • Capital strategy emphasis shifted toward repurchases: Q3 highlighted 6.62 million shares repurchased and an unwillingness to issue equity at a large discount; Q2 included discussion of potential capital raising if possible and deploying into potentially cheaper mortgages.

  • Analyst focus remained consistent across quarters—dividend durability, hedging/funding impacts, leverage management—but Q3 added more direct probing on buyback vs. asset-growth trade-offs.

Risks and Concerns

  • "We certainly have exposure to volatility and mortgage basis" even while being "very well hedged from an interest rate standpoint." (CFO, Chief Investment Officer, Secretary & Management Director Haas)

  • Management cited market-structure stress during the sell-off, including "forced selling by some of the more highly levered investors" and slowing demand from CMO-related buyers, which "put additional pressure" on specified pools. (CFO, Chief Investment Officer, Secretary & Management Director Haas)

  • Management framed valuation as a strategic constraint: "We're not willing to sell shares at anywhere close to this level of a discount." (Chairman, President & CEO Cauley)

Final Takeaway

Management framed Q3 as a quarter dominated by a late-period rates and mortgage sell-off that drove a sharp book value decline, while emphasizing active hedge adjustments, liquidity management, and continued stock repurchases at a sizable discount to book. Heading into Q4, leadership described plans to reinvest paydowns, selectively add mortgage assets as conditions normalize, and keep buybacks on the table, while maintaining that taxable income remains aligned with dividends paid year-to-date and that, at current leverage, the portfolio can generate high-teens ROE.

data.title: AI is enhancing required skills in the labor market rather than displacing roles – Robert Half’s earnings call
data.description:
AI is expanding required skills rather than broadly displacing specialized roles, creating high demand for candidates who combine functional expertise with AI fluency, critical thinking, and sound judgment, according to M. Keith Waddell, vice chairman, president, and CEO of Robert Half (RHI).

"The ability to assess and validate AI-generated outcomes is becoming an increasingly important part of that skill set," he said during the company's earnings call.

However, the increasing reliance on generative AI by job seekers is making it more challenging for employers to distinguish between candidates stated qualifications and demonstrated capabilities, according to Waddell.

He noted that "our ability to identify and validate highly capable talent represents an increasingly important competitive advantage."

AI adoption is driving strong demand for professionals with expertise in technology, data, finance, and business transformation, according to the CEO.

"We are seeing growing demand for highly qualified talent to support this transition," Waddell stated.

data.title: Deckers Outdoor facing near-term headwinds as HOKA, UGG sales slow -- analysts
data.description:
Disappointing fiscal second quarter sales for Deckers Outdoor (DECK) continue to reverberate through the company’s shares as investors weigh the performance of its HOKA and UGG brands against the outlook for the broader athletic footwear market.

Although the company reported record revenue and a 27% increase in profits, the sales miss (first in more than 5 years) and lowered top-line guidance are driving shares as much as 6% lower on Friday and led to a series of price target cuts.

Crucially, Piper Sandler downgraded Deckers Outdoor (DECK) to Underweight from Neutral, citing poor reception to new HOKA offerings, the promotional environment among peers, signs that UGG sales are peaking, and sluggish market dynamics that are expected to last until at least next summer/fall.

Margins were protected by abstaining from promotional pricing, and profitability and capital efficiency “remain hallmarks of the DECK business,” writes Stifel’s Peter McGoldrick. “But the next leg higher in the stock requires reacceleration, particularly in the HOKA brand.”

While both HOKA and UGG remain well positioned for growth in the longer term thanks to new offerings and broader price tiers, the sales guidance cut introduces near-term uncertainty, namely for its direct-to-consumer channel. 

Truist analyst Joseph Civello also raises the question of category saturation in HOKA with FY27 sales now expected to increase by a high single-digit percentage compared to earlier estimates for low double-digit percentage growth.

“This outlook balances sustained strength internationally with ongoing pressures in the U.S.—primarily impacting DTC, as Deckers remains committed to full-priced selling.” 

Although the fiscal second quarter results were mostly favorable, analysts still see uncertainty ahead as full-year estimates optimistically embed “a meaningful acceleration in HOKA, incremental softness in DTC but not a corresponding change in wholesale sales, and new product launches,” BTIG’s Janine Stichter said.

Not to mention that a lot of the company’s future performance hinges on holiday sales “in order to quiet investor rumblings that both brands have peaked,” Needham’s Tom Nikic writes.

Nikic maintains a Buy rating on Deckers (DECK) but lowered his target price by 23% to $96, reflecting the market’s reaction to fiscal Q2 results. 

“This was not a good print,” Nikic says, “as both brands missed Q2 sales and saw their FY outlook cut, leaving DECK shares to languish near-term.”

Friday’s price action pushes Deckers Outdoor (DECK) further into the red for the year and leaves the stock lower for the week for the first time in five weeks.

data.title: American Express reaffirms 10% revenue growth and raises 2026 EPS outlook to $18.30-$18.60 amid restructuring
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: American Express (AXP) Q3 2026

Management View

  • "We had another strong quarter with record revenues of $20 billion, up 9% and EPS of $5.42 reported and $4.68 on an adjusted basis." (Chairman & CEO Stephen Squeri)
  • "Given our strong performance year-to-date, we are reaffirming our revenue growth guidance of 10% and raising our EPS guidance to between $18.30 and $18.60 on a reported basis or between $17.60 and $17.90 on an adjusted basis." (Chairman & CEO Stephen Squeri)
  • "As a result, we took a $336 million charge for restructuring in the quarter, which is expected to result in the elimination of approximately 5% of our positions globally." (Chairman & CEO Stephen Squeri)
  • "Yesterday's announcement of our exclusive partnership with Airbnb... we're excited to bring over 1 million listings globally into our Amex Travel program as well as expanding travel benefits for eligible U.S. card members." (Chairman & CEO Stephen Squeri)
  • "Q3 was another strong quarter, and we continue to see good momentum across the business." (Chief Financial Officer Christophe Le Caillec)
  • "We reported GAAP EPS of $5.42 this quarter, up 31%." (Chief Financial Officer Christophe Le Caillec)

Outlook

  • "We are reaffirming our full year revenue growth guidance of 10% and raising EPS guidance to a range of $18.30 to $18.60 and $17.60 to $17.90 on an adjusted basis." (Chief Financial Officer Christophe Le Caillec)
  • "The fine does not impact our full year 2026 guidance." (Chairman & CEO Stephen Squeri)
  • "The orders do not impose an asset cap on the company and the costs associated with the remediation are not anticipated to affect 2027 guidance." (Chairman & CEO Stephen Squeri)
  • Compared with Q2, management moved from "We continue to expect full year EPS of $17.30 to $17.90" (Chairman & CEO Stephen Squeri, Q2) to the higher Q3 EPS ranges above, while maintaining the 10% revenue growth target.

Financial Results

  • "Revenue was $20.1 billion, up 9% year-over-year." (Chief Financial Officer Christophe Le Caillec)
  • "Net card fee growth accelerating to 17% FX adjusted." (Chief Financial Officer Christophe Le Caillec)
  • "We acquired 3.1 million new cards in the quarter with 76% of new accounts on fee-paying products." (Chief Financial Officer Christophe Le Caillec)
  • "Overall provision expense was $985 million, including a reserve release of $211 million." (Chief Financial Officer Christophe Le Caillec)
  • "In Q3 specifically, we returned $2.2 billion of capital to shareholders, including $1.6 billion of share repurchase and $0.6 billion of dividends." (Chief Financial Officer Christophe Le Caillec)
  • "We ended the quarter with a CET1 ratio of 10.9%, reflecting the gain from the sale of GBTG that happened at the end of the quarter." (Chief Financial Officer Christophe Le Caillec)

Q&A

  • Sanjay Sakhrani, Keefe, Bruyette, & Woods, Inc.: asked about rewards "gamify" risk; Chairman & CEO Squeri responded, "we really don't have a breakage model" and added, "we have levers within our model... we can get to spend thresholds that require those benefits to be made."
  • Ryan Nash, Goldman Sachs Group, Inc.: asked about sustaining spend and mid-teens EPS into 2027; CFO Le Caillec said, "we're not going to get into guidance for 2027" but added VCE should "stabilize" and "help us just like maintain that mid-teens EPS ambition"; CEO Squeri highlighted, "Resy restaurants were up 18%" and "Fine Hotels and Resorts and The Hotel Collection, that's up 50%."
  • Donald Fandetti, Wells Fargo Securities, LLC: asked about premium competition/market share and international moderation; CEO Squeri said international was "22 straight quarters of double-digit growth rate" and added, "we continue to do well, and we're getting the share of revenue that we're looking to get."
  • L. Erika Penala, UBS Investment Bank: pressed on AI-enabled rewards maximization and financial impact; CEO Squeri said, "it's a little too early in the game to determine what the impact will be on VCE" and added Amex will take "a risk-based approach" and allow access only via "approved through API or MCP channels."
  • Bill Carcache, Piper Sandler & Co.: asked if premium competitive intensity feels different; CEO Squeri said, "we really don't see much different than what we've seen" and added the segment expansion has "introduced more people into that part of the TAM."
  • Robert Wildhack, Autonomous Research: asked about allowance coverage ratio; CFO Le Caillec pointed to conservative scenarios and said the 2.6% reserve rate reflects "the premiumization of the portfolio."
  • John Pancari, Evercore ISI: asked about card-fee growth trajectory; CFO Le Caillec said, "we saw that inflection point this quarter" and reiterated, "Again, you're going to have to wait until January for that" on 2027.
  • Terry Ma, Barclays Bank PLC: asked about revolve runway; CFO Le Caillec said borrowing penetration has been "stable" and emphasized, "we're not changing our underwriting approach here."
  • Darrin Peller, Wolfe Research: asked about commercial acceleration milestones; CEO Squeri said middle market is where Amex "have not grown the way we want to grow" and positioned Center plus "more agents" to compete with "Ramp and with Brex."
  • Mihir Bhatia, BofA Securities: asked about the Visa/Mastercard settlement and network strategy; CEO Squeri said, "we've really pivoted" away from "partner with the bigger banks" toward partners like "Synchrony" and "Bread Financial," and added on surcharging, "it doesn't really appear to have affected anybody's business."
  • Cristopher Kennedy, William Blair & Company: asked about banking products; CEO Squeri said, "I think you'll see this continue to play a bigger part in our overall strategy" and noted "the launch this quarter of the business savings account for our small business customers."

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analysts: slightly negative to neutral, centered on potential pressure points (rewards gaming, competitive intensity, reserve conservatism, interchange/surcharging), including explicit framing like "concerns" about rewards being "gamify" (Sakhrani, KBW) and requests for quantification of "financial impact" from rewards maxing (Penala, UBS).
  • Management: slightly positive in prepared remarks and mostly neutral in Q&A; confidence language included "We are on track to deliver another year of 10% revenue growth and mid-teens EPS growth" (Chairman & CEO Stephen Squeri), while uncertainty language appeared on open questions like rewards-maxing economics: "it's a little too early in the game" (Chairman & CEO Squeri).
  • Versus Q2, management tone added more defensiveness/compliance emphasis tied to the OCC action ("we are accountable for addressing them thoroughly" (Chairman & CEO Squeri)), while Q2 emphasized reinvestment choice-making ("We've chosen" to invest rather than drop to bottom line (Chairman & CEO Squeri, Q2)).

Quarter-over-Quarter Comparison

  • Guidance shifted from Q2: "We continue to expect full year EPS of $17.30 to $17.90" (Chairman & CEO Stephen Squeri, Q2) to Q3: "raising our EPS guidance to between $18.30 and $18.60" (Chairman & CEO Squeri), while keeping 10% revenue growth guidance in place.
  • Strategic emphasis broadened from Q2 premium value propositions and partnerships (including TheFork discussion) to Q3’s heavier focus on AI and "Agentic Commerce" plus new travel distribution via Airbnb.
  • Q3 introduced discrete items absent from Q2’s headline framing, including the GBTG transaction gain usage and a restructuring program: "a $336 million charge" and "approximately 5%" headcount reduction (Chairman & CEO Squeri).
  • Analyst focus moved from Q2 sustainability of elevated U.S. consumer spend and reinvestment pacing to Q3’s concentration on AI-driven rewards optimization, competitive pressure in premium, and reserve/CECL framing.

Risks and Concerns

  • "Adjusted EPS includes an expense for legal matters, which includes the unreserved portion of the recently announced civil money penalty levied by the OCC." (Chairman & CEO Stephen Squeri)
  • "The deficiencies cited in the consent orders should not have occurred, and we are accountable for addressing them thoroughly." (Chairman & CEO Stephen Squeri)
  • Management flagged execution and control needs around AI access: "We're just not going to let assistants run rogue through our systems." (Chairman & CEO Stephen Squeri)

Final Takeaway

Management described Q3 as a record-revenue quarter while reaffirming 10% full-year revenue growth and lifting 2026 EPS guidance, alongside disclosing a $336 million restructuring charge tied to an expected ~5% global workforce reduction. Leadership highlighted the Airbnb partnership and a broadened AI strategy spanning acquisition, engagement, payments, and servicing, while stating that the OCC penalty and related remediation are not expected to change 2026 guidance and are not anticipated to affect 2027 guidance.

data.title: Wells Fargo, Arm, Intuit among companies objecting to tokenizing stocks on OKXICE - report
data.description:
Wells Fargo (WFC), Arm (ARM), and Intuit (INTU) have joined a list of companies that are objecting to their shares being "tokenized" on OKXICE, Reuters reported, citing a regulatory document.

Total number of ⁠companies ​that have now objected is 22, the document reportedly said.

OKXICE is a joint venture between crypto exchange OKX and NYSE parent Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) that filed with the SEC to launch a tokenized securities platform for the 24/7 trading of U.S. stocks.

More than 60 listed companies were to be made available. Their shares were set to become tokens that trade on the blockchain via a liquidity pool and offer the same benefits as equities, such as dividends and voting rights.

However, the JV had encountered objections from issuers, the report published on Friday noted.

data.title: Analysts weigh in on Moderna's big drop following cancer vaccine results
data.description:
Moderna (MRNA) closed Thursday down ~17% after phase 3 data was leaked on the company's personalized cancer vaccine, intismeran autogene, and the Street is offering theories on why.

That data showed that intismeran autogene plus Merck's (MRK) Keytruda (pembrolizumab) cut the risk of melanoma returning or death by 42% vs. Keytruda alone, meeting the primary endpoint. The risk of distant metastasis or death, the secondary endpoint, was reduced by 38% compared to Keytruda alone.

One analyst said that the data wasn't as robust as in phase 2. Another stated that the combination could become the standard of care. And a third questioned whether it would become a transformative oncology therapy.

RBC Capital Markets' Lucca Issi, who has a sector perform on shares, noted that phase 2 data for recurrent free survival and distance metastasis free survival were, respectively, 49% and 59%.

Although the phase 2 trial enrolled an earlier cancer stage population compared to phase 3, "Nonetheless, if you look at the [intent-to-treat population] (which is the way the FDA looks at it), the HRs are numerically inferior vs Phase II....Overall, this is not the first time that we have seen impressive Phase II being followed by a more muted benefit in Phase III, but we do believe that this can't be confidence boosting..."

Piper Sandler's Edward Tenthof, who rates Moderna at overweight, said that Thursday's selloff was due to concerns that the standard of care will be neoadjuvant Keytruda. It is important to note that Keytruda has yet to be approved in this setting for melanoma.

"We believe the INTerpath-001 trial appropriately compared againstcurrent SOC and that approval in adjuvant melanoma would be an advantageous label and lead to clinical uptake," he wrote.

Citi's Geoff Meacham provided 10 reasons why, following the data, he doesn't like Moderna's risk/reward. Among them are that positive results do not mean a transformative modality change in treatment, it does not establish an "effective cure," and Moderna's valuation requires more than just the trial results.

"We agree that intismeran looks approvable in adjuvant melanoma, but the bigger picture is that it adds tumor sequencing, manufacturing lead time, treatment coordination and high cost to an already approved and highly effective anti-PD-1 backbone," Meacham wrote.

data.title: Booz Allen outlines FY2027 revenue of $11.3B-$11.6B while raising adjusted EPS to $6.50-$6.70 amid Ultra integration
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Booz Allen Hamilton (BAH) Q2 FY2027

Management View

  • CEO Horacio Rozanski said the quarter stayed aligned with management’s plan: "Booz Allen is on track with the expectations we set for this fiscal year. We delivered strong profitability and cash generation while continuing to invest for the future." (CEO & Chair Horacio Rozanski)
  • Rozanski framed demand as being driven by mission urgency, noting: "demand for advanced technology solutions and products remains strong" while "Artificial or now super intelligence, or SI for short, is powering more sophisticated cyber threats." (CEO & Chair Rozanski)
  • On cyber productization, Rozanski highlighted Vellox and a specific product result: "In testing at scale, Guile reduced attack success rates by more than 95%, and it is currently in private beta with government and commercial customers." (CEO & Chair Rozanski)
  • On Defense Tech, Rozanski emphasized integration plans following the Ultra acquisition: "Now as one company, we will integrate our technologies to address mission gaps faster and more effectively than each of us could do alone." (CEO & Chair Rozanski)
  • COO Kristine Anderson described operating conditions by segment: "National security continued to grow, while civil remained in transition." (COO & President Kristine Anderson)
  • Anderson said contract mix is shifting toward outcomes-based work: "Within national security, our firm fixed price contract mix has increased by 3 percentage points year-to-date." (COO & President Anderson)
  • CFO Troy Lahr summarized execution priorities as including awards, profitability, and cash generation: "I'm pleased with our continued strong operational execution, including capturing strategic awards, delivering profitability above our expectations and generating robust free cash flow." (Executive VP & CFO Troy Lahr)

Outlook

  • Lahr updated FY2027 revenue guidance to "between $11.3 billion and $11.6 billion, implying growth of 1% to 3%." (Executive VP & CFO Lahr)
  • Lahr said the company expects "mid-single-digit growth for the full year" in national security, while Civil is expected to show "a low-double-digit decline for the year, slightly softer than our initial expectations." (Executive VP & CFO Lahr)
  • Lahr raised profitability and cash expectations, stating: "We're raising the bottom end of our prior adjusted EBITDA guidance" to "$1.26 billion to $1.29 billion," and "We're raising our expected adjusted EPS range meaningfully" to "$6.50 to $6.70"; free cash flow is now expected "between $850 million and $925 million." (Executive VP & CFO Lahr)
  • Compared with the prior quarter’s posture of "reaffirming our guidance for the year across all metrics" and waiting to "roll in Ultra" after closing, Q2 included Ultra in guidance and lifted the adjusted EBITDA floor, adjusted EPS range, and free cash flow range. (Executive VP & CFO Lahr)

Financial Results

  • Lahr reported Q2 revenue "declined 3.9% year-over-year to $2.8 billion" and said the change was "largely due to a 10.6% decrease in billable expenses year-over-year" while "revenue ex billable expenses... was down less than 1% versus the prior period." (Executive VP & CFO Lahr)
  • Lahr reported profitability and cash metrics as: "Adjusted EBITDA was $313 million at a margin of 11.3%" and "Adjusted diluted earnings per share increased 18% year-over-year to $1.76"; he added free cash flow was "$263 million." (Executive VP & CFO Lahr)
  • On demand indicators, Lahr said: "We had solid bookings during the quarter with a book-to-bill of 1.5x" and "Total backlog at the end of the second quarter was nearly $41 billion" with "funded backlog... increasing 5% year-over-year to $5.7 billion." (Executive VP & CFO Lahr)
  • On capital deployment tied to Ultra, Lahr stated: "we deployed a total of $965 million" including "$729 million for the Ultra Mission Solutions acquisition" and ended with "$334 million of cash on hand and total liquidity of $1.8 billion." (Executive VP & CFO Lahr)

Q&A

  • Tobey Sommer, Truist: asked about fixed price/OTAs and margin implications; CEO Rozanski said, "the move to outcomes-based is something we embrace" and added the mix of "fixed price or outcome-based" is projected "to continue to grow" alongside "productizing a lot of our IP." (CEO & Chair Rozanski)
  • Gautam Khanna, TD Cowen: asked where funded backlog increased and bookings outlook; CFO Lahr said national security funded backlog "was up 10%" and CEO Rozanski said under a continuing resolution, near-term bookings are "a little harder to predict" due to procurements "shift[ing] to the right." (Executive VP & CFO Lahr; CEO & Chair Rozanski)
  • Louie DiPalma, William Blair: asked Vellox adoption; CEO Rozanski said "it's still early" and added: "the promise of those products will play out much more strongly over the next couple of years than over the next couple of quarters." (CEO & Chair Rozanski)
  • Louie DiPalma, William Blair: asked what scope is removed in Civil recompetes; COO Anderson said it is "how much funding they're actually giving to the same activities" and noted, "there are no significant recompetes remaining for the fiscal year." (COO & President Anderson)
  • John Godyn, Citi: asked if margins can move into a higher regime; CEO Rozanski said, "we expect profit to grow faster than revenue and therefore, margins to expand over the next couple of years," while CFO Lahr cautioned about "lower civil volumes" and "timing of investments" in the next few quarters. (CEO & Chair Rozanski; Executive VP & CFO Lahr)
  • Sheila Kahyaoglu, Jefferies: asked what drives national security acceleration and Ultra contribution; COO Anderson pointed to demand for "battle management solutions" and "space domain awareness," and CFO Lahr said Ultra should have "margins well above the 20%." (COO & President Anderson; Executive VP & CFO Lahr)
  • Matthew Akers, BNP Paribas: asked about headcount stabilization; COO Anderson said, "we added over 300 employees in national security this quarter" and also said the company "will be decoupling growth from headcount." (COO & President Anderson)
  • Scott Mikus, Melius: asked if the growth algorithm still applies and resilience vs. budget cycles; CFO Lahr said, "we are... migrating away from that" and called decoupling "a gradual journey." (Executive VP & CFO Lahr)
  • Seth Seifman, JPMorgan: asked about orders bifurcation and how to dimensionalize cyber exposure; CFO Lahr said the business remains "bifurcated" with national security strength, and CEO Rozanski described cyber as "our most rapidly transforming business" moving toward "technology-first" offerings. (Executive VP & CFO Lahr; CEO & Chair Rozanski)
  • Jonathan Siegmann, Stifel: asked about election-cycle budget dynamics and procurement reform support; CEO Rozanski said reform has "bipartisan" support and added, "we're focused on execution" and "incorporate a variety of scenarios in our guide." (CEO & Chair Rozanski)

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analysts’ tone was slightly negative to neutral, with repeated probing on Civil timing, visibility under continuing resolutions, margin breakout potential, and whether Ultra is material enough to move results, including questions like "how do you think bookings play out" and whether procurements keep "moving to the right." (Gautam Khanna, TD Cowen; Gavin Parsons, UBS)
  • Management tone was slightly positive, leaning confident on medium-term margin expansion and technology differentiation, using language such as "gives me great confidence" and "we expect profit to grow faster than revenue" while still flagging near-term uncertainty around the "continuing resolution" and award timing. (CEO & Chair Horacio Rozanski)
  • Versus the prior quarter’s "cautious optimism" around budget uncertainty and a plan to update guidance after Ultra closed, management in Q2 sounded more anchored to execution with guidance updates already reflecting Ultra and multiple upward revisions. (CEO & Chair Rozanski)

Quarter-over-Quarter Comparison

  • Q2 incorporated Ultra into guidance and raised FY2027 adjusted EBITDA to "$1.26 billion to $1.29 billion," adjusted EPS to "$6.50 to $6.70," and free cash flow to "$850 million to $925 million"; Q1 said the company would "reaffirm" guidance and "include into our guidance in October" what happens with Ultra after closing. (Executive VP & CFO Troy Lahr; CEO & Chair Horacio Rozanski)
  • Q2 messaging sharpened the bifurcation narrative: COO Anderson said, "National security continued to grow, while civil remained in transition," and CFO Lahr said Civil decline was "slightly better than we guided to last quarter" while award timing remains difficult to predict. (COO & President Anderson; Executive VP & CFO Lahr)
  • Analyst focus broadened from Q1’s emphasis on funded backlog improvement and contract-type reform into Q2’s deeper push on margin regimes, Civil scope reductions, Ultra integration economics, and the pace of cyber product adoption. (John Godyn, Citi; Louie DiPalma, William Blair)

Risks and Concerns

  • CEO Rozanski reiterated budget-process risk: "we are now in a continuing resolution" and said near-term dynamics are "something we're watching very closely," especially for how it affects funding and awards. (CEO & Chair Rozanski)
  • Management described ongoing Civil execution risk tied to procurement delays, with COO Anderson stating, "Some of the larger bids are just pushing to the right," and CFO Lahr noting DSO elevation expectations due to acquisitions: "we expect our DSO to remain elevated... due to the Defy acquisition." (COO & President Anderson; Executive VP & CFO Lahr)
  • Integration and investment pacing were positioned as margin variables, with CFO Lahr saying the updated adjusted EBITDA range "implies a step down in margins in the second half" due to seasonality and "timing of investment spending," plus "incremental costs and interest expense associated with the Ultra acquisition." (Executive VP & CFO Lahr)

Final Takeaway

Management presented Q2 as execution tracking to plan despite federal budget uncertainty, emphasizing accelerating cyber and Defense Tech productization (including Vellox and Guile testing results) and the Ultra acquisition as a catalyst for scaling mission-proven defense tech offerings. Guidance for FY2027 was updated to $11.3B-$11.6B in revenue and raised ranges for adjusted EBITDA, adjusted EPS, and free cash flow, while management continued to flag Civil timing and continuing-resolution dynamics as the main near-term swing factors.
